articles.title: Prince William makes surprise appearance on Graham Norton Show
articles.summary: The Prince of Wales was marking his Earthshot Prize, to which all of Norton's guests were linked.
articles.content:
The Prince of Wales has made a surprise appearance on the Graham Norton Show, as part of a special edition to mark the Earthshot Prize.

During the episode, which airs on Friday, he joined Cate Blanchett, Robert Irwin and Hannah Waddingham, who are all involved with the prize.

As Norton spoke about the initiative with the trio he surprised the audience by then inviting the prince out to join them on the sofa, to cheers and gasps from the audience.

They discussed the need to pair optimism and urgency when tackling climate change. The prize was founded by William to "celebrate and scale the solutions that will repair our planet".

The guests also chatted about William's long-time support for Aston Villa, and his love of Christopher Nolan films.

William set up the Earthshot Prize in 2020, drawing inspiration from US President John F Kennedy's Moonshot project, which challenged scientists to get astronauts to the Moon and back safely.

There are five Earthshots, or goals, for which an award is given: Protect and Restore Nature, Clean Our Air, Revive Our Oceans, Build a Waste-Free World and Fix Our Climate. Each winner receives £1m.

The future king has committed himself to the prize until 2030. This year's winners will be announced at a ceremony in Mumbai in November.

Last year, the ceremony for the prizes drew famous faces such as former Formula 1 driver Sebastian Vettel and then-UK prime minister Keir Starmer. Pop stars Kylie Minogue and Shawn Mendes performed at the ceremony in Rio de Janeiro.

The 2025 winners included Lagos Fashion Week, for "transforming one of the world's most wasteful industries" by requiring designers to demonstrate their commitment to sustainability.

At last year's ceremony, William said the winners were "proof that progress is possible".

The Graham Norton Show is on BBC One at 22.40 Friday.

articles.title: Activists celebrate as land given protected status
articles.summary: Volunteers say they have been campaigning for 30 years to keep a wild space free from development.
articles.content:
Campaigners who have been trying to stop the development of a town's green space have celebrated it being given "village green status" by a council.

Harding's Pits, seven acres of land beside the River Great Ouse in King's Lynn, had previously been earmarked for a housing development and a supermarket before the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk applied to Norfolk County Council for the status.

The Harding's Pits Community Association Group has campaigned for the past 30 years to keep the area as a leisure space.

Rick Morrish, 64, the director of the group, said it was a "really great decision... we've struggled to get the village green status for 30 years".

The application was considered by Norfolk County Council's Planning (Regulatory) Committee on Tuesday.

Morrish told Chris Goreham on BBC Radio Norfolk that "this year's administration got right behind" the cause and it would "give more legal status to protect the site... we're safeguarding it as a public open space".

**What happened** – After 30 years of efforts by the Harding's Pits Community Association Group, the land has been officially given "village green status" by Norfolk County Council. This decision was supported by the Borough Council of King's Lynn and West Norfolk and was approved by the Planning Committee on a recent Tuesday.

**Impact** – This new status legally protects Harding's Pits from being developed. It means the land will remain a public space where people can enjoy nature and leisure activities. The decision is a big win for the community, especially for those who have worked for decades to preserve this green area.

**One-sentence takeaway** – After 30 years of campaigning, Harding's Pits in King's Lynn is now legally protected as a village green, securing its future as a public natural space.

articles.title: Project aims to protect rare arctic-alpine plants
articles.summary: The three year scheme is awarded £65,000 to collect seeds and plant them in the fells.
articles.content:
A project aiming to help protect rare arctic-alpine plants is set to launch.

Teesdale Special Flora Research and Conservation Trust has been given a £65,000 grant for a three-year scheme.

It will see volunteers work with the trust to collect seeds and put them on the fells of Upper Teesdale.

The trust's founder, Dr Margaret Bradshaw, said the group wanted to raise awareness of the fragility of special flora in the area.

"This project is crucial to support the ongoing research and conservation of these rare species," she said.

The trust is also raising £15,000 to help support the project.

The North Pennines National Landscape awarded £65,000 to the trust from the government's Farming in Protected Landscapes programme.

The organisation said Upper Teesdale had an "unusually large number of rare plant species", including the Teesdale Assemblage.

This is a "unique community" of 20 rare and endangered arctic-alpine plants believed to have "survived continuously since shortly after the last glaciation", between 10,000 and 12,000 years ago, a spokesman said.

The programme manager for natural heritage at the North Pennines National Landscape, Sarah Tooze, said: "We are looking forward to working with local farmers on ways to support these fragile species."

articles.title: Soaring oil prices underscore the need to help poor countries adopt renewables
articles.content:
War-induced spikes in oil prices and the arrival of artificial intelligence are widening the economic gap between rich and poor countries, according to the International Monetary Fund’s October report on the world economy. Poorer countries that import most of their fossil fuels have suffered the worst consequences of the United States’ and Israel’s war on Iran, while wealthier countries have better withstood war-related shocks thanks to AI-related economic growth and diversified energy systems, the report said.

Renewable and clean energy could help poorer countries strengthen their economies against future economic turbulence, but a well-planned energy transition requires resources these countries don’t have. Instead, families and companies in developing countries are pursuing their own ad hoc energy transitions with cheap electric motorbikes and rooftop solar panels. Demand for an energy transition in poor economies is here, experts say, but no one is providing the planning and money to make it orderly or equitable.

“Getting off oil is the only solution to this long-standing, but currently very acute, economic vulnerability,” said Rebecca Ray, an economist studying global sustainable development at Boston University. “The question is, who’s going to pay for it?”

Oil and gas prices, which have soared as wars in the Middle East and Ukraine have destroyed refineries and closed shipping routes, have made all kinds of products more expensive, including fertilizer and goods that must be shipped with fossil fuel-burning engines. Those high prices hit hardest in poor countries, where people and governments already struggle to afford necessities.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

High fossil fuel prices can also have unwelcome knock-on effects in poor countries, like making it harder for the governments to borrow money. Rising fuel prices slow down an economy, meaning governments take in less tax money. Investors then get skittish about lending to those governments because of their weakened incomes. Governments must then take on riskier loans with steeper interest rates to stay afloat, adding to already high costs of borrowing. That can lock them into financial trouble and make it harder for them to spend on their people.

“The world’s poorest countries are likely to see their productivity and growth momentum decelerate and the gap in their per capita incomes relative to those in advanced economies widen” through the early 2030s, the IMF report states. The report echoes repeated warnings about the global impacts of the war in Iran from international organizations since early in the year.

Still, residents of low-income countries are responding to the crisis by seeking opportunities for resilience. Even before fuel prices spiked from war in the Middle East, private citizens and companies in poor countries were investing in their own renewable energy. The war seems to have accelerated those trends or demonstrated their value.

For instance, electric mopeds and motorcycles now zip through crowded intersections in Vietnam, where their sales nearly doubled after the outbreak of the war, now representing 28 percent of new two-wheel vehicles sold. In Pakistani cities, rooftop solar had effectively doubled the country’s electricity capacity in two years leading up to the war. After the war began, all those solar panels kept the country’s electricity prices fairly stable, shielding the country from the same economic shocks it experienced following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

An energy transition is happening, but it’s not a systematic change. And it’s not equally distributed among the people of poor countries. Installing so much unplanned rooftop solar takes wealthier households off power grids, leaving poorer households to pay for the grids’ improvements. EV growth can strain grids without the appropriate planning and infrastructure improvements. And the organization and expense required for a wholesale energy transition just aren’t feasible for many governments.

Ethiopia, for instance, has rocketed ahead of other African countries to become a global leader in electric vehicle adoption, but the country still only has 13 public charging stations and suffers regular blackouts, making its EV rollout potentially precarious. The country has doubled its national electricity generation with the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam hydropower project, which came online last year, but it still needs a reliable grid to make that power boost meaningful. Nepal, which is also leveraging hydropower to support massive EV adoption — over 70 percent of new vehicles sold — is similarly watching its electric vehicle stock grow faster than the chargers and grid technology needed to support it.

Visitors examine a battery-powered rickshaw during the NAIMA Nepal Mobility Expo 2025 in Kathmandu, Nepal. Cui Nan / China News Service / VCG via Getty Images

Building out essential infrastructure like power grids is exactly the kind of project that international development institutions like the IMF are supposed to invest in. The IMF and World Bank, both headquartered in Washington, D.C., were founded by over 40 allied nations in 1944. Both organizations, along with a series of regional development institutions like the Asian Development Bank, constitute a system whose public goal is to provide loans, research capabilities, and financial advice to developing countries so they can build projects needed to grow their economies. However, throughout their history, both organizations have received criticism for prioritizing debt repayment over well-being within borrower countries, potentially worsening inequality and corporate profiteering.

Today, the largest of these organizations aren’t stepping up to overhaul energy systems in developing countries — in fact, the World Bank abandoned its ambitious climate-related lending goal in June, following the Trump administration’s calls for it and the IMF to refocus away from climate issues. And the large countries that help fund those organizations, like the United States, European nations, and China, have recently reduced their funding for infrastructure development in poor countries.

“Developing countries have been caught in a downward spiral of decelerating growth and increased vulnerability,” said Shekhar Aiyar, director of the Indian Council for Research on International Economic Relations, at an event hosted by the Center for Global Development this month. “At the same time, there has been a vast scaling back of bilateral aid” — that is, aid from rich countries to poorer ones.

Wealthy countries have promised over a trillion dollars to help fund climate-related projects in developing nations by 2035, but annual payments are meant to ramp up and aren’t fully available yet. Plus, wealthy countries have historically failed to meet similar promises.

If there’s a silver lining, it’s that the economic fallout from the Iran war has made the economic importance of transitioning poor countries away from fossil fuels undeniable.

“It’s now more widely understood that decarbonization is a critical goal for macroeconomic stability, and just that recognition is a really encouraging step,” Ray said.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights the urgent need and growing demand for renewable energy adoption in poorer countries to reduce economic vulnerability caused by fossil fuel dependence and geopolitical conflicts. It details real-world impacts such as increased adoption of electric vehicles and rooftop solar in developing countries, showing tangible progress toward a cleaner energy transition. Although challenges remain due to lack of funding and infrastructure, the recognition of decarbonization as critical for economic stability and the grassroots shifts in energy use provide a hopeful and significant narrative with broad societal and environmental implications.
articles.personality_title: Rising oil prices push poorer countries toward renewable energy

People and businesses in these countries are turning to renewable energy options like electric motorbikes and rooftop solar panels, even without government help or big investments.

For example, in Vietnam, sales of electric motorcycles nearly doubled, and in Pakistan, solar power helped keep electricity prices steady during the crisis. Projects like improving power grids and building charging stations for electric vehicles are needed so renewable energy can grow safely and reach everyone.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Rising oil prices are pushing poorer countries to adopt renewable energy, but they need more support to build reliable systems and reduce economic risks.

Les habitants et les entreprises de ces pays se tournent vers des solutions d’énergie renouvelable comme les motos électriques et les panneaux solaires sur les toits, même sans aide gouvernementale ni gros investissements.

Cependant, ces changements sont inégaux et manquent de soutien, ce qui peut créer de nouveaux problèmes comme des réseaux électriques peu fiables et des coûts plus élevés pour les plus pauvres.

Il faut améliorer les réseaux électriques et construire des bornes de recharge pour véhicules électriques afin que les énergies renouvelables se développent en toute sécurité et bénéficient à tous.

articles.personality_title_es: El aumento del precio del petróleo impulsa a los países pobres hacia las energías renovables
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El precio del petróleo ha subido mucho debido a las guerras en Medio Oriente y Ucrania. Esto ha dificultado que los países pobres, que dependen del petróleo importado, puedan pagar la energía y otros productos.

**Qué pasó** – Según un informe reciente del Fondo Monetario Internacional (FMI), los países pobres sufren más por el aumento del precio del petróleo y los problemas económicos causados por estos conflictos. Las personas y empresas en estos países están optando por energías renovables como motos eléctricas y paneles solares en los techos, incluso sin ayuda del gobierno ni grandes inversiones.

**Impacto** – Este cambio hacia la energía limpia muestra que los países pobres quieren depender menos de los combustibles fósiles caros y poco estables. Por ejemplo, en Vietnam, las ventas de motos eléctricas casi se duplicaron, y en Pakistán, la energía solar ayudó a mantener estables los precios de la electricidad durante la crisis. Sin embargo, estos cambios son desiguales y faltos de apoyo, lo que puede causar nuevos problemas como redes eléctricas inestables y costos más altos para los más pobres.

**Próximo paso** – Los expertos dicen que para que esta transición energética sea justa y efectiva, las organizaciones internacionales y los países ricos deben dar más fondos y ayuda para planificar. Es necesario mejorar las redes eléctricas y construir estaciones de carga para vehículos eléctricos para que las energías renovables crezcan de forma segura y lleguen a todos.

**Conclusión en una frase** – El aumento del precio del petróleo está impulsando a los países pobres a adoptar energías renovables, pero necesitan más apoyo para construir sistemas confiables y reducir riesgos económicos.
